analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security by raising benefits, boosting cost-of-living adjustments, and applying payroll taxes to earnings above $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill to expand Social Security and tax high earners' wages above the cap was referred to a Ways and Means subcommittee in February 2017 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1114, the Social Security Expansion Act, would have increased Social Security benefits, changed the annual cost-of-living adjustment to an inflation index that better reflects what seniors actually buy, and applied the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above $250,000 — a group that today stops paying Social Security tax once wages pass the cap. The bill was introduced by Rep. Peter DeFazio with 39 Democratic cosponsors on February 16, 2017, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee. It was sent to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security on March 1, 2017, and no further action was ever taken on it. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019. [S1] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries: retirees, disabled workers, and surviving family members, who would receive larger benefits and annual increases that better track the costs seniors face. Lower- and middle-income workers would also be shielded from any tax increase, since only earnings above $250,000 would become subject to the Social Security payroll tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries; low- and middle-income workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would increase Social Security benefits and change how annual cost-of-living adjustments are computed, using the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, an index built around the purchases of older households, in place of the standard index. [S2] [S3]

It would apply Social Security payroll taxes to net earnings from self-employment and wages above $250,000, so very high earners, who currently pay Social Security tax only up to the annual wage cap, would contribute on income above that level. [S2] [S3]
The bill would deposit the resulting revenue into the Social Security trust funds, shoring up the program's financing while expanding benefits rather than cutting them. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: High earners: individuals whose wages and self-employment earnings exceed $250,000 in a year would pay Social Security tax on the portion above that amount, including through the self-employment tax. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes on high earners and on the self-employed above the threshold, which critics of payroll tax increases argue reduces incentives to work and hire at the margin. [S2] [S3]

Applying payroll tax to earnings above the cap breaks the long-standing link between the amount a high earner contributes and the benefits a formula tied to contributions would otherwise produce, an objection frequently raised by opponents of lifting or raising the cap; the bill addresses this partly by not crediting the new tax years toward benefits for those with earnings above the threshold. [S3]

Switching the cost-of-living adjustment to the CPI for Elderly Consumers raises annual benefit increases across the board, which increases program costs over time; opponents of expansion argue this makes the program's long-term finances harder to balance even with the new revenue. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are broad and slow-moving: bigger, better-inflation-adjusted checks for tens of millions of retirees, disabled workers, and survivors, plus stronger program financing. The costs are narrow and fall only on households with earnings above $250,000. A person who genuinely opposes any payroll tax increase, or who is worried about the CPI-E's higher inflation measure compounding costs, has a real objection — but the bill's design pairs the benefit expansion with its own revenue source, which is more fiscally coherent than expansion on borrowed money.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security a few weeks later, and then sat there; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held before the Congress ended. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 16, 2017, with 39 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support. [S1] [S4]
The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Education and the Workforce Committee, a common step that splits a bill's provisions among panels. [S5]

On March 1, 2017, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security within Ways and Means, and the public record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 115th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners with wages and self-employment income above $250,000 a year, who will continue to pay Social Security tax only up to the annual wage cap, and anyone who preferred that Social Security remain as it is. Current and future beneficiaries will not receive the larger benefits or the senior cost-of-living index the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoided the new tax

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.role: Sponsor (D-OR); introduced the bill and led its 39-cosponsor bloc
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 16, 2017

against.name: Ways and Means Committee leadership (Rep. Kevin Brady, chair)
against.role: Chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, the panel with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to Ways and Means and its Social Security subcommittee, but no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled in the full committee or on the floor during the 115th Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: the sponsor and all 39 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill made no visible progress under the Republican-run committee. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill's funding source is a new payroll tax on earnings above $250,000, so the direct losers are very high earners, who today stop paying Social Security tax once wages pass the annual cap. This group's interest in the bill ran against the benefit expansion for ordinary beneficiaries. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and small business owners above the threshold
industries.note: The bill specifically amends the self-employment tax to apply to net earnings above the $250,000 level, so high-earning independent professionals would pay both halves of the payroll tax on income above the cap. [S3]
